source.title: On layer-level control of DNN training and its impact on generalization

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares generalization across optimizers and training settings, and measures layer rotation as a correlate of test performance. It uses its own controlled training method rather than the original methods in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports layer-rotation curves and test accuracies for multiple tasks. Results cited from other work are not included as rows. Some test-accuracy values are available only in figures.
record.test_reason: The study's own image-classification experiments compare adaptive optimizers with SGD plus weight decay through a shared Layca reference, bearing on V4. It also reports nearly equal training accuracy. Its layer-rotation experiments do not test the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors present layer rotation as a consistent empirical indicator of generalization and propose that it explains effects of learning rate, weight decay, warmup, and adaptive optimizers. They also suggest that layer-level dynamics explain adaptive methods' training-speed advantage. Their feature-learning interpretation is preliminary, and abrupt rotations without training improvement are an explicit exception.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces Layca, which controls layer-wise rotation rates, and studies its relation to test performance across image-classification tasks. Optimizer comparisons use the paper's own training setups; experiments are not the original optimizer studies' recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer rotation rate, relative rotation by layer depth, learning rate, weight decay, warmup duration, optimizer, and Layca control change the reported outcomes. Abrupt rotations that do not improve training loss are an exception to the rotation/generalization trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger, sufficiently uniform layer rotations generally accompany better test accuracy; abrupt rotations without training improvement are an exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-wise cosine distance from initialization predicts generalization in these image-classification experiments when rotations accompany actual learning.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD with weight decay reaches large rotations and test accuracy comparable to the best Layca configuration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay can improve SGD generalization alongside increased layer rotation in these setups.

fits_no_version.finding: Warmup reduces early SGD instability, while Layca trains successfully without warmup in the tested ResNet-110 setup.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controlling early layer rotations can reduce high-learning-rate training instability.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding Layca to adaptive methods brings test accuracy to the level of SGD plus weight decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-rotation control can remove the adaptive-optimizer generalization deficit in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam's second-moment estimates vary predominantly across layers; larger rotations in the MNIST MLP accompany more prominent learned features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer rotation may reflect layer-level optimization dynamics and the extent of feature learning.

fits_no_version.finding: A numerically constrained LARS implementation gives nearly identical accuracy to Layca on three tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some Layca operations can be omitted while preserving its performance in these settings.

record.problems: Most test-accuracy results are shown in figures without exact values in the text; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors note that abrupt layer rotations that do not improve training loss are exceptions to their proposed rule of thumb. Several claims about the mechanisms behind optimizer effects are interpretations of empirical associations.
record.rows_left_out: No result-bearing findings were intentionally omitted. Figure 6's per-method, per-task plotted values were not transcribed as separate rows because exact plotted values are not stated in the text; the five task-level aggregate findings are retained in R19–R23.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level random-label test accuracy alongside natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps through and beyond zero training error.
Matched convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparisons and the role of learned local connectivity or initialization.

Language benchmarks, systematic broad hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and word-level language-model advantages. Layca changes the update algorithm and does not establish what broader tuning of the original optimizers would achieve.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptation of large-batch recipes.
Controlled dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and rankings against norm or margin measures.
Memorization-based example removal versus random removal and retraining.

missing.what: Add training accuracies to the uncontrolled optimizer comparisons: RMSProp/C10-CNN1 100%, Adam/C100-resnet 100%, Adagrad/tiny-CNN 100%, RMSProp+L2/C10-CNN2 100%, and Adam+L2/C100-WRN 99.9%. SGD+L2 reaches 100% on all five. These establish comparable training fit for the V4 comparison.
missing.locator: Supplementary B.3, Tables 4 and 6; amend R19–R23.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any listed version. Figure 6 uses one adaptive method per task, in the caption's stated order. Its text reports an overall deficit, so no unsupported per-task numerical differences or failures are inferred. Layca recovery is an algorithmic intervention and does not by itself warrant a limits_scope verdict on V4's limited-tuning claim. For rows linked to none, cannot_determine means the measure cannot establish a listed version, not that the study's separate finding is unreadable.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Language benchmarks, broad optimizer tuning, optimizer switching, and word-level language models.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized training examples and subsequent test accuracy.

relationships.condition: Uncontrolled adaptive optimizers across five image-classification tasks, with learning-rate search on the first three and source settings on the last two.
relationships.reason: R19–R23 report an overall held-out deficit despite 99.9–100% training accuracy; R11–R15 show SGD+L2 matching the common Layca reference. This supports the qualitative overall pattern, without establishing a deficit for every individual task.
relationships.display_finding: In the unverified comparisons, adaptive methods reportedly performed worse overall on held-out data despite nearly perfect training accuracy, while SGD with L2 matched the Layca reference. The overall results do not establish how the methods ranked on each task.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Five image-classification tasks; adaptive methods without Layca control versus Layca and SGD + weight decay
reader_labels.reason: Uncontrolled adaptive methods have overall worse generalization than Layca's optimum, but adding Layca control brings them to test accuracies on par with SGD + weight decay (R19–R23).
